red.focus: Distinguish obligations imposed by different legal systems
red.summary: Learn why a legal duty always requires identification of the person bound and the recognized rule. Explore duties arising from legislation, promises, and particular relationships across legal traditions.
checklist: I can identify who owes a duty to whom
I can separate moral obligation from enforceable legal duty
I can recognize diverse legal sources of obligation

sections.title: Who Must Do What?
sections.body_md: A company promises to deliver equipment to a hospital. Whether its failure creates a legal claim depends on the applicable contract law, the agreement, and any governing legislation. A legal duty identifies an actor required to do or avoid conduct under an authoritative rule. Different systems recognize similar broad categories—contractual, statutory, fiduciary, public—while defining their elements differently. The first question is not which legal family sounds familiar, but what source creates the particular obligation.

sections.title: Promises and Public Rules
sections.body_md: Some duties arise because persons undertake obligations through recognized agreements; others arise regardless of consent, such as duties imposed by traffic or environmental rules. An agreement cannot necessarily waive a public safety requirement. Equally, a moral promise between friends may lack elements required for legal enforcement. This distinction matters everywhere but the legal tests vary. A careful comparison identifies which duties flow from consent, which from status or conduct, and which from the state's public protective role.

sections.title: Relationship Matters
sections.body_md: A trustee's obligations may be more demanding than those of a stranger in an ordinary market transaction. A professional may owe obligations to a client; parents and children may occupy legally defined relationships. How those duties arise and change differs across systems. A lawyer must not infer fiduciary duties merely because someone trusted another person. Identify the particular relationship, the governing rule, whose interests it protects, and the behavior it requires before making a liability claim.

yellow.focus: Compare obligations, delicts and non-contractual duties
yellow.summary: Move from duty sources to distinct methods for establishing responsibility. Understand why civil-law codes and common-law doctrines may organize similar conduct under different categories.
checklist: I can distinguish agreement-based and non-contractual duties

sections.title: Beyond a Bargain
sections.body_md: A driver who injures a stranger may owe duties of care even though the parties never agreed to anything. Common-law systems often analyze such cases through tort doctrine; civil-law systems may speak in terms of delictual or extra-contractual responsibility. The categories vary, and the terms cannot be translated one-to-one in every context. Identify the actual protected interest, duty standard, fault requirements and remedy. Similar facts can be organized under different doctrinal headings without changing their human stakes.

sections.title: Codes and Cases
sections.body_md: Civil codes may state broad obligations in general provisions, leaving courts to clarify application to particular facts. Common-law systems may derive a duty standard from a combination of decisions and legislation. Both involve interpretation, and neither is exclusively deductive or exclusively case based. For a comparative problem, read the controlling provision or decision in the original system before translating it into another's vocabulary. A familiar label is only the beginning of the legal analysis.

sections.title: Public Duty and Private Claim
sections.body_md: A regulatory safety rule can impose a public obligation without automatically giving every person a private right to damages. Some systems allow a statutory violation to inform civil liability; others require a separate cause of action. Distinguish whether the rule exists, who enforces it, and whether a private claimant can invoke it. Otherwise a legally accurate statement that a company broke a regulation may be turned into an inaccurate promise of compensation to an injured person.

orange.focus: Analyze overlapping duties in transnational transactions
orange.summary: Study how multiple sources may govern the same relationship across national borders. Distinguish choice of law, mandatory rules, and party agreement when duties conflict.
checklist: I can identify governing-law and mandatory-rule questions
I can separate a contractual choice-of-law clause from jurisdiction

sections.title: A Contract Crosses Borders
sections.body_md: An online platform based in one country sells a service to a customer in another. Their agreement may select a governing law, yet consumer-protection rules in the customer's country may still impose mandatory safeguards under applicable private international law. The legal result depends on forum, jurisdiction and specific conflict rules. Choosing a law is not the same as deciding which court may hear the case. A sophisticated lawyer analyzes the choice clause, mandatory limitations, and enforcement route separately.

sections.title: Mandatory Duties Limit Bargaining
sections.body_md: Rules protecting employees, consumers or personal data may restrict the parties' ability to contract away safeguards. The precise protections depend on jurisdiction and sometimes residence, workplace, or targeting of a market. One cannot assert that every domestic mandatory rule applies worldwide. Comparative analysis should explain the connecting factors that make a law applicable, the protected interest it serves, and the conflict rule used to resolve competing obligations.

sections.title: Institutional Duties Travel Unevenly
sections.body_md: International business can involve contractual promises, professional fiduciary duties, public compliance obligations and expectations of responsible conduct that are not all legally enforceable in the same way. A corporation's public ethics policy, for example, may create reputational commitments without necessarily creating a private damages action. A sound legal opinion identifies each normative layer and states what evidence would convert a claim into an enforceable duty. The aim is reliable guidance, not a maximal list of laws.

black.focus: Defend legal duties under unequal power and plural institutions
black.summary: At doctoral depth, examine why duty sometimes exceeds consent in relationships marked by dependency and unequal control. Design comparative obligations that protect vulnerable persons without imposing limitless liability.
checklist: I can evaluate consent as a justification for duty under unequal bargaining
I can compare public regulation and private enforcement
I can defend duty allocation based on control and institutional competence

sections.title: Formal Consent and Real Freedom
sections.body_md: A migrant worker may sign an agreement under conditions of limited language access, urgent financial need and dependence on an employer. A rule treating signature as conclusive consent can overlook structural constraint. Yet disregarding every agreement would also undermine autonomy. A comparative theory should identify which information, alternatives and protections make consent meaningful, and how mandatory duties can correct predictable vulnerability. Actual rights and remedies must come from the governing legal order rather than a moral conclusion alone.

sections.title: Protecting Without Overreaching
sections.body_md: A platform may influence working conditions while denying traditional employer status. Duties could arise from labor law, consumer law, data regulation or tort, each with distinct jurisdictional boundaries. A proposed reform should examine who controls the risk, who benefits, and which institution can realistically monitor compliance. Imposing every possible duty on every participant is neither administrable nor necessarily just. The scholarly task is to justify a proportional allocation that preserves legitimate cooperation while protecting persons with little bargaining power.

sections.title: Plural Obligations and the Client
sections.body_md: A lawyer may owe duties under professional regulation, private contract and ethical commitments to the client's well-being. Those layers should reinforce rather than confuse each other. The legal question asks what rules are enforceable; the professional question asks what honorable service requires where the rules permit discretion. In a cross-cultural setting, genuine respect includes listening, informed consent and clear explanation of choices. Great representation protects a person's freedom to decide, not merely the lawyer's ability to win.
